To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the mixing model is a linear combination of the sources, (2) each receiver is a function of the source locations, (3) the source signals are statistically independent, (4) each receiver records the source signals with different time delays, (5) the source signals have different Gaussian distributions, and (6) the sources can be modeled by a Gaussian mixture model with unknown mixing coefficients.

(1) the mixing matrix can be estimated from data, (2) a simple ICA algorithm can be used to deblend seismic shot records, and (3) the algorithm can be applied to seismic data from simultaneous random sources with unknown wave kinematic relations.

(1) we have extended the applicability of independent component analysis for deblending seismic shot records to cases where the mixing model is more complex than previously assumed, (2) we have demonstrated that independent component analysis can be applied to seismic shot records generated by simultaneous random sources with unknown wave kinematic properties, and (3) we have shown that independent component analysis is a viable tool for deblending random sources in seismic-while-drill experiments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the question of how to decompose seismic shot records into isolated records involving a single source at a time, and how to identify the source location and the corresponding wave kinematics.
the following question: How can we decompose seismic shot records generated with simultaneous sources into isolated records involving each source separately?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

ICA is a powerful technique that is able to separate sources in the presence of complex mixing models, provided that the following assumptions are satisfied: (1) The sources are statistically independent, (2) the mixing model is known or can be estimated, (3) the sources are non-Gaussian, and (4) the sources are not too similar.
ICA can be applied to seismic data with a complex mixing model if the following assumptions are satisfied.

the ICA algorithm works for deblending seismic shot records from simultaneous sources with unknown wave kinematic parameters, provided the sources are sufficiently different and the number of sources is known.

we can deblend seismic shot records with complex wave kinematics, if the sources are statistically independent, the sources have non-Gaussian distributions, and if the wave kinematics can be estimated from the deblended shot records.
the seismic sources are assumed to be statistically uncorrelated, and the mixing model is assumed to be linear, time invariant, and minimum phase.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ICA can be applied to deblending shot records with unknown wave kinematic properties, provided the sources are statistically independent and the mixing model is linear.
the ICA algorithm can be applied to seismic deblending problems without the need for any a priori assumptions on wave propagation, and without requiring the sources to be statistically independent.

ICA can be applied to seismic shot records, provided the following conditions are met: (1) the sources are uncorrelated, i.e., they are independent; (2) the sources are non-Gaussian, which is the case in seismic experiments; (3) the mixing model is known.
